newsitem.title: GREECE: Turkey's Demirel says army is out of politics.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Demirel says army is out of politics.

text.p: President Suleyman Demirel said on Saturday Turkey's armed forces were not involved in the country's deepening government crisis and that Turkey would remain a secular state.

In a two-part interview to Athens' private Antenna television station on Friday and Saturday Demirel said Islamic fundamentalism had no place in Turkey which should soon become a European Union member.

"The army has no relation with politics. The truth is that that in every country when they plan foreign policy they ask the army's opinion in case there is danger and they have to get involved. Their opinion does not mean they exercise foreign policy," Demirel said.

"There is no Islamic fundamentalism in Turkey. This is a secularist and democratic country .... Everything (happening) in Turkey is according to the constitution. Everything is in accordance with the laws."

Turkey's Islamist-led coalition government led by Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan has suffered a number of recent defections to opposition parties and Turkish media have accused it of endangering the country's secular constitution and tradition.
The media have regularly pronounced the government dead and predicted that the powerful secularist military would mount their fourth coup since 1960 to dislodge Erbakan.
Turning to Turkey's relations with the EU Demirel said tense relations with Union-member Greece should not stop Turkey's membership.
"Turkey should be an EU member one way or the other because primarily it is to the interest of both Europe and Turkey. Turkey should not be left out (from the EU's enlargement)."
"It could take years to solve our problems (with Greece) and Turkey should not be excluded from the EU for this reason," Demirel said.
He called for dialogue with Greece to solve territorial differences in the Aegean Sea, something Athens has repeatedly rejected, saying it will not negotiate over its territory.
NATO allies Greece and Turkey have long-standing differences over territorial and mineral rights in the Aegean Sea, the divided island of Cyprus and a Moslem minority in northern Greece.

They almost came to blows last year over two uninhabited islets in the Aegean but have recently agreed to an EU plan calling for committees of experts from both countries to to seek ways of resolving the problems.
Demirel said Cyprus, whose northern third is occupied by Turkish forces since 1974, could not become an EU member before Turkey does.
The EU has agreed with Nicosia's internationally recognised Greek-Cypriot government to start accession talks towards the end of the year.
